title: const references
learningGoals: know when to use const and ampersand

youtube.title: C++ const References: Fast and Safe Parameters | C++ Programming EP 25
youtube.description: In this episode you will pass big values without copying, protect a parameter with const and know when to use const and ampersand, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 const references · 1:17 A const reference · 2:12 Which parameter style? · 3:03 Second program · 4:25 Recap · 4:55 Bug of the Day · 5:52 Challenge · 6:18 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we learn the most common parameter style in modern C plus plus. It is fast, and it is safe.

scenes.onScreen: "const references": numbered lines (1. A copy of a big value is slow; 2. A reference avoids the copy; 3. Const stops the function from changing it) and an analogy card: a museum: you may look at the painting, but you may not touch it
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Copying a big string for every call is slow. A reference avoids the copy. But a reference lets the function change the original. Add const, and the function may only read it. So a const reference is fast and safe. Think of a museum. You may look at the painting, but you may not touch it. Here is the rule of thumb. For small types like int and char, pass by value. For big types like string, pass by const reference. If the function must change the value, use a plain reference. This rule is used in nearly all C plus plus code, so learn it well.
points: A copy of a big value is slow
Const stops the function from changing it

scenes.onScreen: show.cpp: show reads a string without copying it
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The parameter is a const reference to a string. No copy is made. [HL 6] The function may read text, but it may not change it. [HL 11] Main passes the string. [HL 6] The function prints it. Use this style for strings and other big values. [HL 5] Read the type from right to left. Text is a reference, to a string, that is const. [HL 6] If you try to write to text here, the compiler stops you. [HL 11] The call looks normal. Main does not need to know that the function is careful. This protects your data, and it keeps the program fast.

scenes.onScreen: a table of three parameter styles
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Here are three styles. A plain parameter makes a copy and cannot change the original. A reference makes no copy and can change the original. A const reference makes no copy and cannot change the original. For big values that you only read, choose the last style. Notice the three cases in the table. A copy is safe, but slow for big values. A plain reference is fast, but it can change the original. A const reference has both good points, because it is fast and safe.

diagram.caption: a table of three parameter styles

scenes.onScreen: longer.cpp: longer takes two const references
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] Both parameters are const references. Both strings are only read. [HL 6] The function compares the sizes. [HL 12] Panjim and Mapusa both have six letters, so the answer is false. [HL 13] A const reference can also take a plain quoted text. Margao is longer than Goa, so the answer is true. [HL 6] The size function gives the number of letters. We only read the strings, so const is right. [HL 13] A quoted text is not a string yet. The compiler makes a short-lived string for the call. A const reference may hold such a short-lived value, but a plain reference may not.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as longer dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints false and then true. Notice the word false. Panjim and Mapusa have the same size, so one is not longer than the other.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A copy of a big value is slow. Two. A const reference makes no copy. Three. The function may read the value but not change it. Four. A const reference can take a temporary value. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A copy of a big value is slow.
A const reference makes no copy.
The function may read the value but not change it.
A const reference can take a temporary value.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Changing a const reference
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The function takes a const reference, and then tries to add one. The compiler says increment of read-only reference. Const means look, but do not touch. If the function must change the value, remove const. This error is useful. It says that you tried to change a value that you promised only to read. You have two choices. If the function should change the value, remove const and use a plain reference. If not, delete the line that changes it.

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

bump.cpp: In function 'void bump(const int&)':
bump.cpp:5:5: error: increment of read-only reference 'n'
    5 |     n++;
      |     ^
bug.why: A const reference is read-only. If the function must change the value, use a plain reference. If it must not, remove the change.

pun: "The museum guard loves const references. He says, look all you want, but do not touch the exhibit."
challenge: Write a function that prints the size of a string. Choose the best parameter style, and explain your choice in a comment. Hint: a const reference to a string is the right choice here.
challengeAnswer: Use const string ampersand. The function only reads the string, and a reference avoids a slow copy.
